note_on_method: This is a state page, so most of it is a claim about coverage rather than about a court. Where it describes a place, the source is that operator's own publication - the City of Cape Coral's Park Sports/Games page, the City of Tampa's pickleball page, the City of Tallahassee's pickleball page. Where it describes what is missing, it names the city we looked at and says why it is not here, because 'not listed' and 'does not exist' are different things and a reader deserves to know which one they are reading. Statements about cities we read and declined - Fort Myers, Orlando, and the five that answered a 403 - are statements about our own access and rules on one day, not about those cities' courts. This page exists because Tallahassee was published on 7 September 2026, making Florida the third state with three verified cities. Nobody working on this has played on any court in Florida.

slots.coverage:
Florida has sixty-seven counties. This page covers three cities in three of them.

Twenty-eight venues, 106 courts, three municipal operators, one to a county. Hillsborough County holds sixteen of those venues and 52 of the courts, all inside Tampa. Leon County holds seven venues and 34 courts, all inside Tallahassee. Lee County holds five venues and 20 courts, all inside Cape Coral. Every venue here is run by a city parks department, and not one private club, gated-community court, church gym, school or commercial facility appears. That is a statement about who writes court counts down rather than about where pickleball in Florida is played.

Florida is the third state on this site to have a page of its own; North Carolina and Washington came first. A venue publishes when its operator states a court count and an address that resolves, a city when three or more of its venues do, and a state when three of its cities do; Tallahassee, published on 7 September 2026, was Florida's third.

The three cities arrived by three different documents, and the differences matter more than the totals. Cape Coral, read on 4 September 2026, publishes one Park Sports/Games page that states a count, a lighting answer and a price for every venue it lists - "Two (2) tennis courts -OR- Four (4) pickleball courts with lights - open until 9:00 p.m. daily" - and prices all of them in one sentence: the City's park tennis and pickleball courts are "available for public use at no charge". Tampa, read on 7 September, publishes a grid of cards dated "Updated: 10/28/2025", one per venue, each carrying a label, a name, an address and a count, with an "Indoor Pickleball" heading over the community-centre gyms; because the label and the heading are the City's own words, indoor or outdoor is stated for all sixteen venues, and lighting, price and surface are stated for none. Tallahassee, read the same day, publishes one page that gives each outdoor venue an address, a count line in the City's words and a weekly schedule, then defines its own vocabulary beneath: Open Play sessions "do not require a fee", Reserved Play costs $4.25 to $5.75 a session, and First-Come First-Play "just means that the court is open", with a 90-minute limit when others are waiting. Two of its counts are the City's own two-figure arithmetic - LeVerne Payne's "2 courts with adjustable net straps, 4 courts with portable nets if needed and all have painted lines", Tom Brown's "4 pickleball courts | 8 pickleball courts on multi-purpose courts (tennis courts 1-4)" - and both publish as the sum.

What the three cities refuse is as much a part of the record as what they publish, and it is named rather than dropped. Eleven venues on the three Cities' own pages are absent. Six carry a stated count and fail on an address: The Courts in Cape Coral, "32 dedicated pickleball courts and 12 tennis courts" with no address published by the City at all; Gator Trails Park, two lighted dedicated courts at "3628 Garden Blvd", found by neither resolver; Rowlett Park in Tampa, eight courts at "2401 E Yukon St.", found by neither; Foster Park, two courts at "4700 S Clark Ave., 33611", which the Census answers as North Clark Avenue in a different postcode; the Dr Martin Luther King Jr. Complex, two indoor courts under two City house numbers, 220 and 2200 N Oregon Ave; and Four Oaks Park in Tallahassee, six courts "used for pickleball only" at "5151 Four Oaks Boulevard", found by neither. Those six hold 52 stated courts between them, nearly half again the 106 published. Five more are refused for want of a number: Cape Coral's Four Freedoms Park, a "portable indoor court" priced at $5 and never counted, and four Tallahassee indoor centres - Lawrence-Gregory, Lincoln Neighborhood Center, Sue Herndon McCollum and the Tallahassee Senior Center - each on the City's indoor schedule with sessions and never a court count.

Beyond the three, seven more Florida cities have been read and none has published, for reasons that belong to our access and our rules rather than to their courts. Fort Myers publishes a count for one venue, the Racquet Club's six courts, and its facility directory serves five facilities to a fetcher and pages the rest by script. Orlando keeps counts and addresses on different pages and yields two solid venues where three are needed; the third is a table row reading "4 - pickleball" at "East Park" with no directory page behind it. Naples, Sarasota, St. Petersburg, Clearwater and Gainesville answered a plain request and a full browser header set with an HTTP 403 or a bot challenge on 7 September 2026, and nothing publishes from a page that cannot be snapshotted and re-checked; a 403 is a fact about one day, and those five are where the next Florida attempt starts. Jacksonville, Miami, Fort Lauderdale, Pensacola, Lakeland and the rest of the state have not been read at all, which is a statement about a reading list rather than about their courts.
slots.seasonality:
The honest headline is that the three Florida operators state almost nothing about seasons, and this page will not supply the missing part from memory. What they do state falls into three kinds: closing times, lights, and schedules that move with the calendar.

Cape Coral writes the rule once for all of its park courts: they are open "from sunrise to sunset (or later for locations with lighting)". Sunset is the one closing time that moves through the year, so that sentence is the closest thing to a seasonal statement any Florida operator makes. Three parks are then written past it: Camelot, Jim Jeffers and Joe Stonis are "with lights - open until 9:00 p.m. daily", fourteen courts whose closing time does not move. Giuffrida Park is written the other way, "Two (2) dedicated pickleball courts  - no lights", so its two courts close at sunset whenever sunset is. Sands Park's four carry no lighting answer either way and are recorded as unknown rather than dark.

Tampa states no lighting for any of its sixteen venues, and states hours for three of its twelve outdoor ones. Madison Street Park and Vila Brothers Park are "Open daily from sunrise to sunset". The New Tampa Sports Pavilion prints "Monday-Friday, 4:30-9 pm / Saturday-Sunday, 8 am-9 pm", the one outdoor closing time in the city that runs to a clock rather than to the sun; the City does not write the word lights beside it, and neither does this page. The other nine outdoor parks state neither, so the evening question has no answer there.

Indoors, Tampa is the one operator in Florida whose schedule names a season, and the season is summer camp. Its seven indoor courts sit in five community centres that are pickleball venues only during printed sessions, and the sessions are written around the camp: Loretta Ingraham runs Monday and Friday 6:30-8:30 pm "Until Summer Camp begins" and Mondays only "Beginning June 2"; Cordelia B Hunt runs Tuesday 6:45-8 pm and Thursday 6-6:45 pm "Schedule through June 1", then shorter evenings "June 2-August 8"; Forest Hills and the refused Dr Martin Luther King Jr. Complex both carry "Play resumes after Summer Camp ends"; Port Tampa's card adds "Court closed for repairs through June 1". None of those dates carries a year, on a page the City dates 28 October 2025, so the pattern is more reliable than the dates: a Tampa gym is a court until the camp moves in. Barksdale is the exception: weekday afternoons, Monday 1-3 pm with free beginner lessons then 3-5:30 pm and Tuesday to Friday 2-5:30 pm, with no camp note.

Tallahassee states its calendar by the month, and only at Winthrop Park. The City warns that "the GA/FL A and B league will be utilizing 5 courts on Tuesdays and 6 courts on Thursdays from 9:00am-12:00pm (September through April)", and that "local school teams will be using the courts from 3:30-5:00pm (January through April)". Winthrop has six courts, so on a Thursday morning from September to April the league has all of them. The City's clinics run in six dated sessions across the year, Session 1 from January 12 to March 4 and Session 6 from October 12 to December 2, at Tom Brown on Monday and Wednesday evenings and at LeVerne Payne on Wednesday mornings; no year is printed beside them. Jake Gaither carries the one outdoor hours line in the city, printed here as the City prints it, "Outdoor FCFP: 8:00am - 9:00pm Daily, Closed on Sunday". Walker-Ford carries the one lighting statement, "3 courts - night play is available", which is published as a lighting answer on that phrase.

Put the three together and the state's evening picture, on what can be verified, is this: four venues stated lit, holding seventeen courts - Camelot, Jim Jeffers and Joe Stonis in Cape Coral and Walker-Ford in Tallahassee; one venue stated unlit, Giuffrida's two courts; and twenty-three venues, including all sixteen in Tampa, where the operator says nothing either way. Lit courts and indoor courts are what make play after dark possible - reasoning rather than data, and the one sentence about evenings written here without a source.

The indoor count is smaller than the indoor picture. Eight of the 106 verified courts are indoor: seven in Tampa and one at Jake Gaither in Tallahassee, Reserved Play only on Friday middays. Cape Coral has no published indoor court because the City counts none - Four Freedoms Park's "portable indoor court" in "air-conditioned comfort" is priced at $5 per person for two hours and never numbered - and Tallahassee runs indoor Open Play and Reserved Play at four more centres that publish sessions and no counts. The indoor programme in Florida is larger than the indoor inventory on this page, and the gap is in what gets written down as a number. What no operator states is a rain policy, a heat policy, a summer closure or a surface, and until one of them writes one down this section stays as short as it is.
slots.notable:
Tom Brown Park in Tallahassee is the largest verified pickleball site in Florida, at twelve courts, and the twelve is the City's own arithmetic in two kinds: "4 pickleball courts | 8 pickleball courts on multi-purpose courts (tennis courts 1-4)". Four stand alone; eight are lined onto four tennis courts. The City says which you get: "pickleball professionals have priority to use courts 1A/1B for teaching purposes during non-monitored hours", and the "Open Play schedule includes combo courts 4A-4B and the four standalone pickleball courts". Open Play there is free and drop-in on Monday, Wednesday and Sunday mornings and Sunday evenings; Reserved Play, at $4.25 to $5.75 a session, fills Monday to Thursday evenings and Tuesday, Thursday and Saturday mornings; Friday is first come, first play. It is one of two published venues the City takes online reservations for, with Winthrop.

Macfarlane Park is the largest set in Tampa at eight outdoor courts, and it holds that rank because the City's other eight, at Rowlett Park, sit at an address neither resolver can find. Cuscaden Park's six carry the one scheduled outdoor session in Tampa, "Senior open play Wed 9-11 am". Julian B Lane Riverfront Park's six are the most precisely described courts in the city - "2 permanent courts" and "4 portable net courts" - which tells you before you go that four of the six may have no net on them when you arrive.

Two Florida venues have courts on both sides of the indoor line at one address. Forest Hills in Tampa has two outdoor courts and two indoor, on two City cards for one building at 724 W 109th Ave, the indoor pair on a schedule that pauses for summer camp. Jake Gaither Community Center in Tallahassee is written by the City as "1 indoor court, 2 outdoor courts", the outdoor pair first come, first play to 9:00pm and the indoor court Reserved Play on Friday middays. Tampa has more published indoor venues than any city on this site, though Bellevue has more indoor courts: five centres, seven courts, every one a gym that is a pickleball venue only during its printed sessions.

The most notable venue in Florida is not published, and it is worth being exact about why. The City of Cape Coral lists The Courts with "32 dedicated pickleball courts and 12 tennis courts", more than the whole of published Cape Coral, and it is the largest count of any venue this site has read and then refused. The City publishes no address for it and gives it no park page, so there is no municipal record of where it is; and it sits underneath the City's sentence that its park courts are "available for public use at no charge" while being a paid facility on its own operator's account. Four Oaks Park in Tallahassee is the same shape at a smaller size: six courts "used for pickleball only", Open Play and Reserved Play seven days a week to 10:00pm, online reservations, and an address, "5151 Four Oaks Boulevard", that neither resolver finds. It is the flagship of the City's programme and it fails on its address alone.

Giuffrida Park in Cape Coral is notable for a single line: "Two (2) dedicated pickleball courts  - no lights". It is the one stated lighting negative in Florida, and it is the reason the silence at Sands Park, four dedicated courts with no lighting answer, is recorded as unknown rather than read as a no. Sands and Giuffrida hold the six courts in Cape Coral the City calls dedicated; the other fourteen are on tennis slabs written as "Two (2) tennis courts -OR- Four (4) pickleball courts", and Jim Jeffers adds "two (2) warm-up pickleball courts" to reach six, the largest set in that city.

LeVerne Payne Community Center in Tallahassee tells you the most about its nets - "2 courts with adjustable net straps, 4 courts with portable nets if needed and all have painted lines" - and is where the City schedules "Beginner & Adv. Beginner Open Play" on Tuesday, Thursday and Saturday mornings, free, and its Wednesday-morning clinics at three levels. Lafayette Park's two courts come with the one equipment loan stated anywhere in Florida: "paddles and balls available inside the Sue McCollum Community Center only during regular office hours".

Few cities on this site carry a verified free court, six at the time of writing, and two of the six are in Florida. The other four are Portland, Scottsdale, Boulder and St. George. Cape Coral's five venues are free by one City sentence. Tallahassee's LeVerne Payne and Tom Brown are free because the City schedules Open Play there and writes that "all Open Play sessions are drop-in and free"; its other five venues are first come, first play at no stated price, which is not the same as free. Tampa's fifty-two courts carry no price at all, and the one "free" on its page prices a beginner lesson at Barksdale rather than a court.
slots.growth:
Nothing in Florida is published as growth, and this page will not describe it as growth on its own authority. No Florida operator on these pages prints a conversion date, a construction notice, a bond, a planned court or a count history. What the three Cities do print is a set of dates, two maintenance notices, one programme and one arrangement of tennis courts, and each says something if it is read carefully and not past its edges.

The dates first. Tampa's pickleball page is dated "Updated: 10/28/2025" and its recreation-centres list "Updated: 05/21/2026", so when the pickleball page was read on 7 September 2026 the count-bearing record was more than ten months old and the phone-number record less than four. Every session on the pickleball page is written without a year - "Beginning June 2", "June 2-August 8", "Court closed for repairs through June 1" - which is why those schedules are read here as the City's last statement rather than this week's promise. Tallahassee's page prints a notice on the far side of its own date: "Due to scheduled resurfacing, both the outdoor tennis and pickleball courts at jack mclean will be unavailable for use until december 5, 2025." That date had passed nine months before the page was read, and the sentence was still there. It is published as the City prints it and asserted on every build, so the day the City removes it the page is read again. The same schedule marks Lincoln Neighborhood Center as "No Pickleball (renovations in progress)" on every day of the week, with no count and no date. Two courts resurfaced, one court repaired, one centre under renovation: that is the whole construction record in verified Florida.

The programme is Tallahassee's, and it is the clearest evidence on these pages of a city organising demand rather than merely housing it. The City runs clinics in six dated sessions across the year - seven or eight weeks each from January to May and from mid-August to early December, four weeks each in June and from mid-July - with registration open for the first two at the time of reading; it gives its "pickleball professionals" priority on courts 1A and 1B at Tom Brown "during non-monitored hours"; it publishes a skill-rating scheme; and it writes a rotation rule for busy Open Play - "If 6 players are waiting, players will play 9 points instead of 11 points", after which all four players come off. The City also takes reservations online through Court Reserve at three parks and by phone on 850-891-4940, at $4.25 to $5.75 a session with a senior rate from 62. None of that changes the thirty-four; it is what a programme looks like once a count has been settled.

The arrangement is Cape Coral's. Three of its five parks are written as "Two (2) tennis courts -OR- Four (4) pickleball courts", and the park pages say the same thing from the other side: "Two (lighted) Tennis Courts that include court lines for Pickleball". One slab, two configurations, and which one you find depends on who set it up last. Six of the City's twenty courts are dedicated, at Giuffrida and Sands. The pattern is the usual one - lines on tennis courts first, dedicated courts in smaller numbers - and the thirty-two dedicated courts at The Courts, unpublished for want of an address, would change the pattern's shape if the City ever wrote down where they are. Tampa's arrangement is similar and less described: Julian B Lane's "2 permanent courts" and "4 portable net courts", Davis Islands' "2 multi-purpose courts", and "courts" without a qualifier everywhere else, which this page does not read as dedicated.

What would change this page most is not construction but a record. Inside the three cities, five addresses stand between 50 stated courts and publication - The Courts, Gator Trails, Rowlett, Foster and Four Oaks - and a resolvable address for any of them promotes it the day it appears; the Dr Martin Luther King Jr. Complex waits on the City choosing between its own two house numbers. Outside them, the queue is Fort Myers and Orlando, each short of three venues, and the five cities that refused a fetcher on 7 September, which will be tried again because a 403 is a fact about one day. Every Cape Coral, Tampa and Tallahassee page this state page rests on is snapshotted into the repository that builds it and re-asserted on every build, so if Tampa moves its "Updated" date, Cape Coral drops the "no lights" at Giuffrida, or Tallahassee publishes a count for the Senior Center, the build fails and someone reads the page again.

faqs.q: How many pickleball courts are there in Florida?
faqs.a: Nobody can tell you honestly, and this page will not pretend to. What has been checked is 106 courts across twenty-eight venues in three cities - Tampa with 52, Tallahassee with 34, Cape Coral with 20 - each with a named source and a date. The three Cities' own pages name eleven more venues, six of them holding 52 stated courts, that fail on an address or a missing number.

Because three is how many have an operator that states a count and an address for three or more venues on a page we can read. Fort Myers publishes a count for one venue; Orlando yields two solid venues and a table row; Naples, Sarasota, St. Petersburg, Clearwater and Gainesville refused a fetcher with an HTTP 403 or a bot challenge on 7 September 2026. Jacksonville, Miami and most of the state have not been read, which says nothing about their courts.

faqs.q: Where can I play indoors in Florida?
faqs.a: On eight verified courts. Seven are in five Tampa community centres - two each at Forest Hills and Loretta Ingraham, one each at Barksdale, Cordelia B Hunt and Port Tampa - each on a printed session schedule, some of which pause for summer camp. One is at Jake Gaither in Tallahassee, Reserved Play only on Friday middays. Tallahassee schedules indoor play at four more centres and Cape Coral prices one indoor court at Four Freedoms Park; none of those publishes a count.

faqs.q: Is it free to play in Florida?
faqs.a: At seven of the twenty-eight venues, and confirmed rather than assumed. Cape Coral states that its park courts are "available for public use at no charge", which covers all five. Tallahassee's LeVerne Payne and Tom Brown are free because the City schedules Open Play there and writes that "all Open Play sessions are drop-in and free"; Reserved Play costs $4.25 to $5.75 a session. Tampa publishes no price for any court, and Tallahassee's other five venues none for first-come play, so those read as unknown.

Four venues, seventeen courts. Camelot, Jim Jeffers and Joe Stonis in Cape Coral are "with lights - open until 9:00 p.m. daily", fourteen courts between them. Walker-Ford in Tallahassee is "3 courts - night play is available", published as lit on that phrase. Giuffrida Park is stated unlit. All sixteen Tampa venues, Sands Park in Cape Coral and six Tallahassee venues carry no lighting answer, which means nobody has said, not that the courts are dark.

faqs.q: What is the biggest pickleball site in Florida?
faqs.a: Tom Brown Park in Tallahassee, at twelve courts - four standalone and eight lined onto tennis courts 1 to 4, in the City's words. Macfarlane Park in Tampa follows at eight, then a group of sixes: Cuscaden and Julian B Lane in Tampa, LeVerne Payne and Winthrop in Tallahassee, and Jim Jeffers in Cape Coral. The larger site is the unpublished one: The Courts in Cape Coral, thirty-two dedicated courts with no address the City prints.

faqs.q: Can I book a court anywhere in Florida?
faqs.a: In Tallahassee, at two published venues. Tom Brown and Winthrop take Reserved Play bookings online through Court Reserve or by phone on 850-891-4940, at $5.75 singles and $4.25 doubles with lower rates from age 62; Four Oaks does too but is not published. Everything else is drop-in: Tallahassee's other venues are first come, first play with a 90-minute limit when others wait, Cape Coral publishes no booking route for its park courts, and Tampa's pickleball cards mention no booking at all.

faqs.q: What does "Open Play" mean in Tallahassee, and why does it decide the free answer?
faqs.a: The City defines three kinds of court time. Open Play "is a Drop-In session in which players simply drop-in, without advanced reservations", and "These sessions do not require a fee." Reserved Play "must be scheduled for a specific time", and "All Reserved Play sessions require a fee payment." First-Come First-Play "just means that the court is open", with a 90-minute limit when others are waiting, and no price stated. A venue reads free here only where the City schedules Open Play.

Cape Coral's pages were read on 4 September 2026 and Tampa's and Tallahassee's on 7 September. All are static web pages that change without notice, so each is snapshotted into the repository that builds these pages and re-asserted on every build. If Tampa changes its "Updated: 10/28/2025" date, Cape Coral removes "no lights" at Giuffrida, or Tallahassee takes down the McLean resurfacing notice, the build fails and the page is read again.

After a game is over, all 4 playing players will switch out to allow 4 new players a game."; Reserved Play "is a court reservation that must be scheduled for a specific time", "All Reserved Play sessions require a fee payment."; "Court Reservations and Fees Singles - $5.75 Singles Senior* - $4.75 Doubles - $4.25 Doubles Senior* - $3.50", "To qualify for the senior rate, you must be at least 62 years of age"; "Court reservations can only be made for Reserved Play sessions, as all Open Play sessions are drop-in and free. Make a reservation online for Four Oaks Park, Tom Brown Park or Winthrop Park - or make a phone reservation by calling 850-891-4940"; First Come First Play "just means that the court is open and people can play any way they would like. If other players are waiting to use the court, there is a 90 minute court time limit." Indoor schedule: "Indoor courts do not have First-Come First-Play available"; Lincoln Neighborhood Center "No Pickleball (renovations in progress)"; Tallahassee Senior Center "$3 Donation Encouraged"; Jake Gaither Friday 12:00pm-2:00pm "Rerseve Play Only". Clinics: "Clinic Sessions Session 1 - January 12 - March 4 (8 weeks) Session 2 - March 23 - May 13 (7 weeks - off April 12-19) Session 3 - June 1-24 (4 weeks) Session 4 - July 13 - August 5 (4 weeks) Session 5 - August 17 - September 30 (7 weeks) Session 6 - October 12 - December 2 (7 weeks - off November 23-28) Registration is now open for Sessions 1 & 2", "Beginner Tom Brown - Mondays & Wednesdays, 6-7 p.m. LeVerne Payne - Wednesdays, 8:30-9:30 a.m."; skill ratings: "With a simple number, you can determine if you want to get involved in a certain game based on your opponent's skill level."
